title: Even the body stays
hookLine: the body you check in the mirror every day stays behind too; a hadith next door says what walks on
tomorrow: five lines the Buddha said to recite often. what are they?

lines: IF IT STAYS, WHAT GOES ON?
cards: Mirrors, gym selfies, skincare steps, the hair that won't sit right: the body gets checked all day long. It's the one possession that feels like me. So if even the body stays behind, what goes on?
The Buddha answers with a plain picture. And a neighbor tradition, Islam, answers with a funeral walk.

teach.b: The Dhammapada's picture is blunt. Before long, this body will lie on the ground, cast aside, without awareness, like a useless log. It isn't said to shame the body.
It's the last of the third root's three steps: wealth stays, the people we love can't come along, and even the body stays.
What goes on, in the Buddha's teaching, is kamma: the intentions a person acted on, and what they shaped. Now the neighbor.
Muslims hand down a hadith, a saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari.
Three things follow the dead to the grave: family, wealth and deeds. Two go back home, and one stays with the person: their deeds. Hear how close that is.
Family turns back at the graveside. The wealth goes home with the heirs. What walks on is what the person did.

A Buddhist could nod at every word of that walk. And one honest difference. In Islam, Muslims believe deeds are brought before God, who judges with mercy, and that God will raise the dead on the Day of Resurrection.
The Buddha's teaching has no judge: deeds bear their own fruit, the way seeds do, and the body left on the ground isn't raised again.
Two neighbors, standing at the same graveside, agreeing on what walks on, and seeing different roads ahead.

how: Buddhist teachers pair Dhammapada 41 with gentle body practices so the reflection leads to gratitude, not disgust; at Muslim funerals, family and community walk the body to the grave, and the hadith of the three that follow is sometimes recalled.

games.q: what does “even the body stays” mean?
o: at death, the body too is left behind
the body stays young if the mind is kept calm
a practice of sitting still for a whole day

games.q: what stays, what walks on — tap the pairs.
p: a body like a useless log

s: Buddhism and Islam see what happens after death in exactly the same way
both say deeds walk on; Muslims believe God judges and raises the dead, and the Buddha's teaching has no judge.
a hadith says that of the three that follow the dead, only deeds remain with them
Sahih al-Bukhari: family and wealth go back; deeds stay with the person.
the 'useless log' verse is meant to make people hate their bodies
it's the last step of the third root: even the body stays. the practice that follows is gratitude.

games.q: at a friend's grandfather's janazah, a Muslim funeral, she tells you the hadith of the three that follow. she asks if Buddhists see it the same way. what's fair?
o: close on what walks on: deeds. different on what's ahead: God's judgment, or kamma with no judge.
exactly the same; every religion teaches this about death.
not at all; Buddhists don't think deeds matter after death.
games.why: shared: family and wealth turn back, deeds walk on. different: Muslims believe God judges and raises the dead; the Buddha taught deeds bear their own fruit.

practice: Rest one hand on your chest and one on your belly, and feel the body breathing under them, a borrowed thing doing its work for now. With each out-breath, let a quiet thank you go to it.
One day it stays behind; today, it's carrying you.

wordCard.voice: Even the body stays: at death the body is left behind too. What goes on is what a person did.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: body; the last thing the third root says stays behind.

carryVoice: A line to keep: even the body, so thank it while it carries you. Day sixteen thirty-seven, held.

sources.ref: Dhammapada 41 (before long this body will lie on the earth, cast aside, without consciousness, like a useless log)
Sahih al-Bukhari 6514 (three follow the dead: family, wealth and deeds; two return and one remains, the deeds)
the third root's three points (wealth, loved ones and the body cannot help at death), as taught in the Tibetan lamrim
